Asif, you keep forwarding me these 'sure-shot' tips. Let me, Karthik, the boring one in this office, tell you how I stopped reading them.
With my first salary, I got a pitch every week. A chit scheme, a friend's 'guaranteed' plan, a man selling plots. Each time I had to decide on the spot, and each time I felt stupid and pressured.
So one Sunday I wrote my own rules on a single page and kept it in my wallet. One: small amounts, every month, same day. Two: only products a regulator watches, the ordinary kind, spread across many companies. Three: anything that promises a fixed high return, I don't even discuss.
After that, pitches got easy. A man at a wedding told me about 'eighteen percent assured'. I didn't have to think. Rule three. I smiled, ate my payasam and changed the subject.
So, Asif, write your page first. Then stop forwarding me things.

qa.a: Anything that promises a fixed high return, Karthik doesn't even discuss.

The fifth call came during dessert. Pradeep listened for ten seconds, heard 'guaranteed twenty percent', said, 'Not for me, thank you,' and hung up. He felt oddly light. The napkin went into his wallet.

subtype: Approach: learn the basics of returns and risk first [Thinking]

In Gautam's village near Sangli, everyone's idea of investing was the same: gold, or the chit fund run by the man at the bus stand. When his classmate Seema mentioned a 'crop-bond' paying 24 percent a year, Gautam realised he had no idea how to judge it.
So on Sunday, on the slow phone signal at the edge of the sugarcane field, he read the beginner pages on the investor education website run by the market regulator. It took two hours. He kept pausing and saying things aloud to the buffalo, who didn't care.
'Bank deposit, low return, low risk. Shares, more return over years, but they can fall. So if someone promises high return and no risk...' He stopped. 'Then either they're wrong or they're lying.'
The next day he asked Seema one question: 'What happens to the 24 percent if the crop fails?' Seema didn't know. Neither, it turned out, did the person selling it.

qa.q: What return did the 'crop-bond' promise?
qa.a: 24 percent a year.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel when Seema first mentioned the crop-bond?
qa.a: Unsure and a little uneasy, realising he had no way to judge whether it was good.

qa.a: How to check whether a product or seller is registered, so the next offer can be checked as well as understood.

qa.a: Caught off guard and perhaps a bit embarrassed, then curious, since the seller could not answer either.

I'm Rukmini, Karthik's flatmate. The day the startup let him go, he came home at three in the afternoon and lay on the sofa without taking his shoes off. For two days he mostly said 'I'm fine' and 'I don't know'.
On the third evening he sat at the dining table with a notebook and started counting aloud, and I listened from the kitchen. 'Savings, ₹84,000. Severance, one month, they said ₹40,000. So ₹1,24,000.' Then: 'Rent share ₹11,000, food ₹6,000, phone and travel ₹2,000, loan EMI ₹5,000. Twenty-four a month.' He divided. 'Five months. A little more.'
He looked up at me. 'Five months,' he said again, differently. Like it was a size, not a monster.
I can't know what was going on inside him. But he took his shoes off that night, and in the morning he was up before me, rewriting his CV.

'Okay. List,' Joseph said, pulling a chair up to Shankar's laptop. 'Since Friday you've said "I'm finished" nine times. Let's do something instead.'
'Fine. Subscriptions first.' Shankar scrolled. 'Two video services, music, a cloud plan, the gym.'
'Which do you actually need?'
'Cloud, for my CV files. That's it.' Click, click. 'Cancelled four. That's ₹1,650 a month.'
'Phone?'
'I'm on the ₹899 plan.'
'You're home all day now. The ₹299 one has enough data.'
'Switched.' He breathed out. 'Now the hard one. The bike loan.'

'And say what? I got fired?'
'Laid off. Say that. Ask what they can do.'
Shankar dialled. Twelve minutes on hold, then a quiet conversation. He hung up. 'They'll move three EMIs to the end of the loan. There's a small charge. I have to email the layoff letter today.'
Joseph grinned. 'So now you've got time to actually look.'

I'm Chetan. The day after the layoff, I didn't apply anywhere. I did something my friend Yamini had done in her own layoff: I looked at what was leaving my account every month.
It was worse than I thought. A video service, a music app, a food-delivery membership, a gaming pass. ₹1,900 together. I cancelled all four before lunch. Then I called my phone company and moved from the ₹749 plan to one for ₹349.
The hard call was the education loan. My EMI was ₹6,800. My hand was shaking while I waited on hold. I explained I'd been laid off and asked what options there were. The officer said I could apply for a three-month moratorium with proof of job loss, though interest would still add up. I sent the letter that evening.
By night I'd cut about ₹2,300 a month and paused the biggest payment. I slept properly for the first time that week.

I'm Anjali. I was laid off on a Monday in March, and by Thursday I had accepted a new job. I remember the relief. I didn't ask about hours, or the probation terms, or even what the role really involved. It paid ₹6,000 less, but I told myself a job is a job.
Keerthana, my closest friend from college, asked on the phone, 'Did you see the contract?' I said it was fine. I hadn't read it.
The role was night-shift data work, not the analytics I'd trained for. The contract said I couldn't leave for six months without paying back the joining costs. By May I was sleeping through the day, eating badly and applying to other jobs in secret on my phone.
Keerthana didn't say 'I told you.' She just helped me read the next offer properly, line by line.
I'm not angry at myself any more. I was scared. But the fear chose that job, not me.

Career counsellor's note, 3 June. Francis, alumni placement office.
Nandini first came to us in February, two days after her startup closed. She was shaking and said she'd take anything. Farhan, you've been refreshing that job site all morning. Sit down. When I was twenty-two, and yes, I'm talking about Suraj, the old man at the corner desk, my first company shut in a week.
For a month I did what you're doing. Refresh, sigh, sleep late. Nothing happened.
Then my neighbour, a retired schoolteacher, made me write a weekly plan on the back of a calendar. Monday: fix one part of the CV. By Wednesday: ten applications, properly read, not blind clicks. By Friday: message five people I'd worked with. Saturday: one mock interview with a friend.
Replies were slow. Some weeks, none. But every Saturday I could tick the boxes, and that kept me sane. In the seventh week, one of those five messages turned into an interview. That's how I got here.
So. Take a calendar, Farhan. Monday, CV. Go.

It's been three weeks since the layoff, and I want you to know I'm okay. Not fine, but okay.
The first week I just replayed it. Then I tried a different question: what are companies actually hiring for right now? I read about forty job posts for backend roles and made a tally. Twenty-six asked for cloud skills. I had almost none.
So that's the plan. I've started a cloud certification course, about ₹9,000 for the exam, and I study four hours every morning. In the evenings I've taken a small freelance job fixing a website for a coaching centre, ₹12,000 for the month. It doesn't replace my salary, but it keeps something coming in, and it's real work to show.
I still wake up at 3 a.m. some nights, worrying. The reframing didn't make that go away. It just gives the worry somewhere to go.
Tell Maa not to worry too much.
Akash

subtype: Approach: seek support from a peer network and a counsellor [Action]
passage:
When the call centre in Hubballi shut its second floor, forty people went home the same afternoon. Nandini and Parveen, who had sat side by side for two years, didn't want to disappear into their houses.
So on Monday they started meeting at the old bus-stand library. Parveen brought a notebook for openings; Nandini brought everyone's phone numbers. By the third week, eleven of them came. They shared leads from the town's shops and banks, and took turns asking each other interview questions under the ceiling fan.
But Nandini was sleeping badly and crying in the bathroom so her mother wouldn't hear. Parveen noticed her eyes one morning. 'There's a counsellor at the district hospital on Thursdays. Free. I went last month.'
That Thursday Nandini went, with Parveen waiting outside. She told her mother that evening too. The next Monday she ran the mock interviews herself.

qa.q: How many people came by the third week?
qa.a: Eleven of them came.

qa.q: Why was Nandini crying in the bathroom?
qa.a: She felt low and overwhelmed after the layoff, and ashamed to let her mother hear.

qa.q: What else could the group add to support each other?
qa.a: A simple check-in on how everyone is feeling each Monday, so people can ask for help early.

qa.q: How might Parveen feel waiting outside on Thursday?
qa.a: Probably quietly worried but glad, having seen the same counsellor and not wanting Nandini to face it alone.

grounding: Shows laid-off colleagues forming a peer group for leads and mock interviews, and one seeing a counsellor when her mood is low.
